section_summary: This section documents U.S. concern about Japanese government finance during the conflicts in Manchuria and Shanghai, including proposed foreign loans, bond refinancing, military appropriations, and external indebtedness. It contains congressional correspondence, State Department cross-reference sheets, fragments of financial reports and telegrams, and material on Japanese government-backed securities. The closing memorandum links the Seiyūkai Cabinet change to the Manchurian crisis and reviews British concern about Japan’s departure from the gold standard, yen depreciation, and renewed textile competition.

subfiles.title: Letter opposing American participation in an international loan to Japan
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: McFadden urges the State Department to prevent American bankers from financing Japanese military activity against China.
subfiles.summary: Citing press reports of possible American and British cooperation on an international Japanese loan, McFadden asks the Department to forbid direct or indirect participation by American international bankers. He requests notification of any application and argues that the matter should be submitted to Congress before action is taken. He connects financial involvement with the danger of U.S. entanglement in the Japanese-Chinese conflict.

subfiles.title: File note for telegram no. 70 on the Japanese government's financial position
subfiles.about: The note directs readers to a telegram concerning the Japanese government's financial position and the cost of military operations.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference points to telegram no. 70 in another decimal-file classification. It characterizes Japanese government finance as a serious problem and warns that military costs could embarrass responsible Japanese officials.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch no. 1490 on French bank loans to Japan
subfiles.about: The note references a German despatch enclosing or discussing newspaper comment on large French bank loans to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This sheet directs readers to despatch no. 1490 under file 862.24/111. The referenced material concerns large loans extended to Japan by French banks and newspaper commentary about them.

subfiles.title: Government Finances—Financial Measures
subfiles.about: The report describes emergency Japanese appropriations and changes to national-bond sinking-fund deposits following dissolution of the Diet.
subfiles.summary: On January 23 the Finance Minister submitted two draft Imperial ordinances to the Throne, including an appropriation of approximately ¥20.9 million for the Manchurian affair. The second measure would reduce deposits into sinking funds for national bonds. Dissolution of the Diet and failure to enact the 1932–33 budget required referral to the Privy Council and approval by Imperial ordinance.

subfiles.title: File note for telegram no. 75 requesting a report on Japanese conditions
subfiles.about: The note references a telegram requesting a report on Japan's current economic and financial situation.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet points to telegram no. 75 under file 894.50/54. The telegram requested a report on contemporary Japanese economic and financial conditions.

subfiles.title: Secretary of State correspondence with Thomas W. Lamont on Japanese bond financing
subfiles.to: Thomas W. Lamont, New York City
subfiles.about: The correspondence reviews Japanese government and government-backed bond transactions, including refinancing and support for the yen.
subfiles.summary: Stimson thanks Lamont for his letter and accompanying financial information. The attached material describes British offers to refund the Imperial Japanese Government's 1905 sterling loan, much of which remained outstanding and some of which was held in the United States. It also discusses the government-guaranteed Taiwan Electric Power Company bond issue and bonds supplied through the Government Deposits Bureau to the Yokohama Specie Bank in connection with a J. P. Morgan loan used to support the gold-based yen.

subfiles.title: File note for telegram no. 107 on budget and Manchurian expenditures
subfiles.about: The note references a telegram on loan authorization and Japanese budget expenditures arising from the Manchurian Incident.
subfiles.summary: The Diet had passed a bill authorizing a loan of ¥67.5 million. The Finance Minister sought ¥7.57 million for Manchurian expenditures during the remainder of fiscal 1931–32 and ¥59.51 million for the opening of fiscal 1932–33.

subfiles.title: Continuation of telegram no. 107 on budget carryovers
subfiles.about: The telegram fragment reports an Imperial ordinance carrying budget appropriations into fiscal 1932 and corrects an earlier fiscal-year label.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports that an Imperial ordinance issued on March 12 carried appropriations from the current budget into fiscal 1932. He refers to a budget outline transmitted with despatch no. 437 and corrects its dates from 1930–31 to 1931–32. The telegram notes that Japan's fiscal year begins April 1.

subfiles.title: File note for telegram no. 107 on Japanese foreign indebtedness
subfiles.about: The note references a telegram concerning Japanese balances and outstanding indebtedness abroad.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram concerned financial balances held abroad and other Japanese external liabilities. It states that the commercial attaché was unable to obtain exact information on these matters.

subfiles.title: File note for despatch no. 517 on military appropriations
subfiles.about: The note references a report on Japanese appropriations for military action in Manchuria and Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: This file note points to despatch no. 517 under another decimal-file classification. The report covered appropriations for the Army, Navy, and other services connected with military operations in Manchuria and Shanghai.

subfiles.title: New Seiyūkai Cabinet in Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes confidential London reporting on the Cabinet change in Japan and British economic concerns about yen depreciation.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Embassy contacts in London reportedly said the Cabinet change was directly connected with the Manchurian question and that civilian efforts to restrain the Army might have provoked a coup. Britain was concerned that Japan's abandonment of the gold standard, loss of gold, and falling exports to China would end a temporary British textile advantage. Yen depreciation, weakening of the Chinese boycott, and Japan's advance purchase of cotton were expected to revive Japanese competition in India and China, prompting British employers to seek longer hours and lower wages.
